Counter-Picking: When and How to Pick Into Someone

Counter picks win lanes when they're used well and lose games when they're not. Learn what makes a counter, when comfort beats it, and how to use a last pick for the whole team.

What a counter pick really is

A counter isn't magic. A champion counters another when something in its kit removes the opponent's way of winning. Usually that's one of four things:

AdvantageHow it worksExample
RangeYou hit them from a distance they can't answerCaitlyn bullies short-range Vayne
Hard lockdownYour crowd control shuts down their all-in or their escapeYasuo's Wind Wall can't block Malzahar's ultimate, which locks him down
MobilityYou dodge the skill shots they depend onAhri's Spirit Rush against immobile, skill-shot mages
All-in powerYou win the fight once it starts, before they scaleKai'Sa with an engage support against Caitlyn

Every champion guide on this site lists tough and favorable matchups, based on current ranked data. Use them as a starting point.

Counter pick vs comfort

Matchup charts assume both players know their champions. In real games, experience often matters more than the matchup. A champion you've played hundreds of times, where you know every power spike and cooldown, will often beat a 'counter' you've played five times.

A simple rule: only counter-pick with champions already in your pool. If your pool is Ahri, Malzahar and Lux, your counter-pick decision is just: which of these three is best into this opponent?

Pro tipBuild your pool so your champions cover each other's weaknesses. Ahri struggles into Katarina; Malzahar (whose passive blocks burst and whose ultimate stops her) handles assassins better. Two champions that cover each other are better than five random ones.

When not to counter-pick

  • When it breaks your team. Countering the enemy mid with an AD champion is a bad trade if your team is already all AD.
  • When the opponent can swap lanes. Flex picks like Ziggs (mid or bot) can change lanes after you counter them.
  • When the 'counter' is weak this patch. Winning lane with a champion that falls off can still lose you the game.
  • When you'd lose to the enemy's jungler. A short-range counter into an aggressive gank jungler might never get to play its lane.
Common mistakeDon't lock in a counter you've never played in ranked. Learn it in normal games first, or you'll lose the matchup you were trying to win.

Reading the enemy's draft

Pay attention to what the enemy picks early. A first pick that's a flex champion, like Ziggs (mid or bot), or a champion that can go top or jungle, means you don't know their lane yet. Wait to counter until you're sure, or pick something that's fine against both options.

Also watch the enemy's hovers and bans. If the enemy bans Malzahar and Annie, their mid probably plays an assassin who hates crowd control. You can plan your pick before they even lock in.

Finally, think about the enemy jungler. If they picked an early-game ganker like Lee Sin or Elise, a lane counter with no escape can be a trap: you win the 1v1 but lose to the 2v1. A safer pick with an escape might be better.

Making the most of last pick

Last pick is a big advantage, and it's about more than your lane. You can see four enemy champions, often all five, so you can:

  1. Counter your lane with the best option from your pool.
  2. Fill your team's gaps. No frontline? No magic damage? The last pick fixes it. See Team Synergy: Building a Comp That Works.
  3. Answer the enemy plan. Against three assassins, pick crowd control and self-peel. Against a scaling comp, pick something that wins early. See Reading the Enemy Team: Pick and Build Against It.

If you pick early, ask your last-pick teammates to cover what you can't.

Synergy in bot lane and with your jungler

Bot lane is a 2v2, so the support and ADC picks work together. An engage support like Nautilus, Rell or Alistar pairs well with an ADC who can follow up: Kai'Sa's passive even stacks faster when allies immobilize enemies, and her ultimate dashes straight onto them. An enchanter like Lulu or Janna wants a hyper-carry like Jinx to protect.

Mid and jungle work together too. A mid with fast wave clear (like Ziggs or Malzahar) can push and move first to help the jungler invade or fight for scuttle and drakes. If your jungler is an early-game champion, pick a mid who can join those fights.

Practice your drafting

Drafting is a skill like last-hitting: the more situations you've thought through, the faster and better your picks become. Before your next session:

  • Read the When to pick box and the matchups tab on each champion in your pool.
  • Write down your one blind pick and which champion you play into assassins, poke and tanks.
  • Test yourself with real scenarios in the Draft Practice tool.

Then use what you learned in lane with the Matchups, Cooldowns & Lane Priority guide.

Key takeaways

  • Counters come from range, lockdown, mobility or all-in power that removes the opponent's plan.
  • Only counter-pick with champions you already know well.
  • Don't counter-pick if it breaks your team's damage balance or leaves you open to flex picks and ganks.
  • Last pick can counter a lane, fill team gaps and answer the enemy plan, all at once.
  • In bot lane, pick a duo that works together: engage with follow-up, or an enchanter with a hyper-carry.
